texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Q: I’m new to product management and I worry sometimes that I’m frustrating or annoying my team without knowing it. I want to avoid that, while still delivering impact. What should I be watchful for?
texts.text: Q: I’m new to product management and I worry sometimes that I’m frustrating or annoying my team without knowing it. I want to avoid that, while still delivering impact. What should I be watchful for?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Product managers appear to be the most disliked function in tech. Case in point:
texts.text: Product managers appear to be the most disliked function in tech. Case in point:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: PMs are often seen as unempathetic, narrow-minded and, worst of all, unnecessary. This makes me sad. But it also tells me that many people simply haven’t worked with a great PM. In my experience, great PMs make everything better: They unblock blockers, stamp out uncertainty, keep everything organized, get your team more resources, protect you from constant flux, align everyone behind an inspiring mission; the list goes on. Once you’ve worked with a great PM, you’ll never want to go back.

Once you’ve worked with a great PM, you’ll never want to go back.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: But PMs often shoot themselves in the foot (and thus make all PMs look bad) by being, as you suggested, annoying. Especially new PMs who need to learn how to deliver results, without any real authority, under pressure.

texts.orig: 1. Obsessing over frameworks, processes and the “right way” to do product
texts.text: 1. Obsessing over frameworks, processes and the “right way” to do product

texts.label: text
texts.orig: By far the best way to annoy your teammates is to obsess over the “right way” of building product, especially by treating a specific framework or process that you read about on Twitter (or certain newsletters 👀) as gospel.
texts.text: By far the best way to annoy your teammates is to obsess over the “right way” of building product, especially by treating a specific framework or process that you read about on Twitter (or certain newsletters 👀) as gospel.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You can tell you’re annoying people in this way when no one around you is making an effort to learn more about, or helping you implement, the framework/process/system. Or it feels like they’re just going through the motions. Or worse yet, people make passive-aggressive jokes about your favorite framework or process.
texts.text: You can tell you’re annoying people in this way when no one around you is making an effort to learn more about, or helping you implement, the framework/process/system. Or it feels like they’re just going through the motions. Or worse yet, people make passive-aggressive jokes about your favorite framework or process.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My advice to you is to absolutely try stuff out, and continue learning from the experience of smart people sharing their wisdom, but remember that it’s more important to have a team that is bought-in and excited about your ways of working than having the perfect process.
texts.text: My advice to you is to absolutely try stuff out, and continue learning from the experience of smart people sharing their wisdom, but remember that it’s more important to have a team that is bought-in and excited about your ways of working than having the perfect process.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The next best way to annoy your team is to prioritize work without people understanding why it’s being prioritized. Particularly when (it feels like) you’re making decisions off anecdotal data. A few examples from that same Twitter thread:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Your teammates care a lot about what’s being prioritized, because their careers are in large part riding on the success of the team. If they don’t believe that what they’re working on will have a significant impact, their work (and morale) will suffer.
texts.text: Your teammates care a lot about what’s being prioritized, because their careers are in large part riding on the success of the team. If they don’t believe that what they’re working on will have a significant impact, their work (and morale) will suffer.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You can tell this is an issue when teammates frequently ask you why something is being prioritized, or push back on the task’s priority. It’s normal for this to happen, say, 10% to 20% of the time, but if you’re getting pushback more than 50% of the time, you’re probably annoying (and losing the trust of) your team.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The next best way to annoy the heck out of your team is to suggest that everything you want them to do is going to be real
texts.text: The next best way to annoy the heck out of your team is to suggest that everything you want them to do is going to be real

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Everyone you work with—engineers, designers, data scientists—also wishes every project could be super-quick. And maybe it could be. But everyone’s burned by promising something will be super-quick and then having to work late nights to deliver it. Instead of suggesting something will be quick, ask, “What would need to be true for this to be doable in the next x days?”

Instead of suggesting something will be quick, ask, “What would need to be true for this to be doable in the next x days?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A fourth excellent way to annoy your team is to avoid making a decision, especially until you reach a consensus. Many PMs desperately want to get to a consensus because they worry about upsetting people or being wrong. In practice, this approach just won’t work long-term, and if you ask people, they’ll often tell you that they’d rather you just make a call and move on.
texts.text: A fourth excellent way to annoy your team is to avoid making a decision, especially until you reach a consensus. Many PMs desperately want to get to a consensus because they worry about upsetting people or being wrong. In practice, this approach just won’t work long-term, and if you ask people, they’ll often tell you that they’d rather you just make a call and move on.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: “Most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90%, in most cases, you’re probably being slow.” —Jeff Bezos
texts.text: “Most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90%, in most cases, you’re probably being slow.” —Jeff Bezos

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Try this next time you’re stuck on a decision: Ask your team if they’d rather keep hashing it out or for you to just make a call. I bet you they’d rather just move on.
texts.text: Try this next time you’re stuck on a decision: Ask your team if they’d rather keep hashing it out or for you to just make a call. I bet you they’d rather just move on.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Another tactic you can use is to say, “It seems like we’re not going to get to a consensus here. It happens! I vote we go with x, move forward, see how it goes and change course if necessary. Everyone OK enough with that?”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A final way to surely annoy your team is to be overly prescriptive about what to build. Basically, leave zero room for creative thought.
texts.text: A final way to surely annoy your team is to be overly prescriptive about what to build. Basically, leave zero room for creative thought.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There’s a fine line between articulating the important details of a project spec and spending three pages explaining one button. This annoying habit can apply to both the beginning of a project, telling designers and engineers exactly how a feature needs to work, and also at the end when you spec out each feature for days.
texts.text: There’s a fine line between articulating the important details of a project spec and spending three pages explaining one button. This annoying habit can apply to both the beginning of a project, telling designers and engineers exactly how a feature needs to work, and also at the end when you spec out each feature for days.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You can tell this is annoying your team if your specs are longer than any other PMs’ you work with, if your designers and engineers don’t really use your documents, or if you hear from your manager that your team is feeling micromanaged.
texts.text: You can tell this is annoying your team if your specs are longer than any other PMs’ you work with, if your designers and engineers don’t really use your documents, or if you hear from your manager that your team is feeling micromanaged.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: My advice is simple: Prioritize conversation over documentation. It’s easy to default to more documentation and detail every time one of your teammates misunderstands something. Instead, use that experience to narrow in on what types of nuances need to be clarified in writing vs. discussing. Don’t assume more writing and documentation will solve these problems.
texts.text: My advice is simple: Prioritize conversation over documentation. It’s easy to default to more documentation and detail every time one of your teammates misunderstands something. Instead, use that experience to narrow in on what types of nuances need to be clarified in writing vs. discussing. Don’t assume more writing and documentation will solve these problems.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As a PM, you are 100% guaranteed to annoy people. You’re in the line of all communication, you’re dealing with people all day, and you have to make complicated decisions under stress daily.
texts.text: As a PM, you are 100% guaranteed to annoy people. You’re in the line of all communication, you’re dealing with people all day, and you have to make complicated decisions under stress daily.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Being self-aware enough to know this puts you ahead of many PMs. I hope that the pointers above put you even further ahead, and make you a less annoying PM—for the good of your team and for all product-management-kind.
